verdicts.note: The direction is clear: 26 years in law enforcement, 10 inside the sheriff's office, and the outgoing sheriff's endorsement [S1][S3][S4]. But he is a lieutenant, not the incumbent, and has no elected or enacted record [S4]. -2 is the maximal proven-record case (long tenure, enacted record); an endorsed internal successor sits at -1, as the treasurer race's 12-year office manager does.

Staffing, analytics-directed enforcement against violent, gang, drug and property crime, prosecution follow-through and continued Flock use [S4], alongside promised prevention programs [S2]: enforcement-leaning but mixed, so -1 medium holds.

He runs explicitly as an outsider to the sheriff's office with no elected record [S1][S3], which points to pole_b. But he has seven years as a police officer, including a period as a sergeant [S1][S3][S4], so he is not the maximal outsider/renewal case; +1.

First-year priorities are youth (Police Athletic League, deputies in classrooms), domestic-violence victims and senior fraud, plus community-engagement policing [S1][S3]; he also wants more deputies through grants [S3], which keeps it at +1 rather than +2. Medium holds.

Weak fit, kept at low: the advisory public vote on Flock cameras is a direct-democracy device and the 'commitment ledger' is a self-accountability pledge [S2][S3]; neither is about campaign money or structural political reform, and his opponent also says he would respect a ballot decision (jake-church.md S4). Low confidence keeps it out of alignment math, which is appropriate.

missing.basis: Would trade in the sheriff's $130,000 Ford Bronco, questions year-end spend-down of budgets and presents the 9.2% rise in the 2026 sheriff budget as something voters should question [S2][S3]; restraint-and-scrutiny proposals (pole_a), tempered by wanting grant-funded deputies.
